analysis.one_liner: Eliminates the FCC rule barring one company from owning a local newspaper and broadcast station.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in December 2016 and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which never acted on it before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal rules currently prohibit one company from owning both a daily newspaper and a full-power radio or TV station in the same town. This bill would wipe out that ban entirely and order the FCC to strike it from its rulebook within a year. It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and died there when the Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.who_benefits: Companies that own newspapers or broadcast stations, especially larger chains that could combine a paper and a TV or radio station in the same market to cut costs and concentrate advertising revenue in one place.

how_it_helps.text: The bill voids the FCC's broadcast/newspaper cross-ownership ban, which bars a single entity, or parties under common control, from owning a daily newspaper and a full-power commercial AM, FM, or TV station in the same market.
It orders the FCC to complete all actions needed to remove the rule from its regulations within one year of enactment.

analysis.who_pays: Local news audiences. In markets where one company buys both the paper and the stations, residents would get one voice covering local news, civic affairs, and politics instead of several independent ones.

drawbacks.text: Allowing common ownership of a town's newspaper and its broadcast stations reduces the number of independent voices covering local government and civic life in that market.

Many struggling newspapers have argued the rule should be relaxed because combining print and broadcast operations could save local papers from closing; wiping the rule out entirely addresses that problem but also clears the way for consolidation in healthy markets where no rescue is needed.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: There is a real good-faith argument here: newspapers are in financial trouble, and cross-ownership restrictions can block arrangements that keep a local paper alive. But this bill did not craft a careful exception for failing papers — it deleted the rule outright for every market, which benefits large station and newspaper operators first and risks thinner local news coverage everywhere else.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced with a bipartisan group of seven cosponsors, sent to the Energy and Commerce Committee, and sat there until the session ended three weeks later.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the House on December 7, 2016 and referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day.
No further action was taken before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017, so the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Local news audiences come out ahead in the narrow sense that the cross-ownership ban stayed on the books, so no market moved toward a single owner of its paper and stations. The outcome mostly reflects timing: the bill arrived in the final weeks of a Congress and had no realistic path.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one; it died quietly in committee

for.name: Rep. Greg Walden
for.role: U.S. Representative (R-OR), bill sponsor and member of the House Energy and Commerce Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on December 7, 2016 to eliminate the FCC's newspaper/broadcast cross-ownership rule.

for.name: Three House Democrats and four House Republicans
for.role: Original cosponsors (Reps. Yarmuth, Green, Rush, Bilirakis, Olson, Guthrie)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill as original cosponsors at introduction.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no further action on the bill after referral; it never received a hearing or committee vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The seven original cosponsors split 4 Republicans and 3 Democrats, and there was no recorded opposition before the bill expired in committee.

industries.note: The bill would have let station owners and newspaper owners buy each other out within the same market, concentrating advertising revenue and news production in fewer hands. In towns where one company ends up owning the paper and the stations, residents lose independent local coverage.

Big companies with both broadcast and print holdings stand to gain most from a market-by-market wipeout of the rule, since they have the capital to acquire local papers and stations quickly. Their interest in this bill runs against media diversity for the public.
